title: A few inches of daylight
note:
The gap has to be small and unmistakable — a few inches, a bright vertical slot. A door drawn a third open is a different rung, and the next two are the ones that own the open door.

The continuity:room reference to door-cover.png was removed before the first restyle round. Every rung carried both it and the continuity:ladder reference to the rung before, and their instructions contradict each other on the one thing the ladder cannot get wrong: the ladder role says match the previous rung's camera exactly, and the room role says match door-cover's camera exactly — but door-cover is a different shot, with the door open and the guest in it. Two attachments arguing about the camera is the shape of the round-1 failure. The previous rung is the room reference, and a better one: the tan-era record shows the camera holding to four pixels across four generations when each frame was attached to the last and nothing else competed. door-stay-03-onestep keeps its door-cover reference because it is the head of the ladder and has no previous rung to use instead.

The camera clause was added after round 22 of door-stay-03-handle drifted: the floor line dropped 29px, the door top rose 10px and the door widened, while the three rungs before it had held the floor line to two pixels. The ladder attachment alone did not hold it. Stating the framing as proportions of the frame put it back to the pixel on the next round.

The gap was described as a measurement — 'no wider than her hand' — which is the exact phrasing docs/pilot-prompts.md records as failing on dg-16: it came back as a shut door with a hand resting on the edge, the same picture as the handle rung before it, and took two goes. The recorded lesson is that when a step's whole subject is a small physical difference, you describe the difference and not the measurement — so this now asks for a full-height stripe of daylight and a door leaf standing proud of its frame, and says a shut door is a reject. Re-declared for cool-flat-v2 (the plaster wall) on 2026-09-04; drawn off the v2 handle.
scene: Interior entry hall, side view, camera at standing eye level. This is the same room, the same camera position and the same distance from the viewer as the other rungs of this ladder: Lucy's rectangular cool-grey dog bed on the left, the closed charcoal front door on the right, and a clear span of taupe-grey floor between them, with the whole walk from bed to door visible in frame. Lucy lies on the bed in a settled down — elbows and hips on the bed, head up and level, watching calmly. Her size in frame, the bed's position and the camera never change between these pictures. No leash. THE CAMERA DOES NOT MOVE: keep the framing of the attached previous rung exactly. The line where the wall meets the floor runs straight across the picture at 62% of its height, so the wall fills the upper five-eighths and the floor the lower three-eighths. The door's top edge sits at 9.5% of the frame height and the door occupies from 75% to 93% of the frame width. Do not zoom in, do not lower the camera, and do not enlarge the door. Only one thing changes from the previous rung: the handler has pulled the front door open a few inches and holds it there. THE DOOR IS VISIBLY OPEN, and this is the thing the picture exists to show. A bright stripe of pale daylight runs the FULL HEIGHT of the doorway, from the top of the opening down to the floor, with a hint of spruce foliage beyond it. The door leaf stands proud of its frame — its leading edge and its thickness are both visible, swung toward the viewer, so the door reads as a slab that has moved rather than a line on the wall. The stripe is narrow, a few inches: not a third open, not half open. A SHUT DOOR IS A REJECT — if this picture could be mistaken for the previous rung, where the door is closed and her hand is simply resting on the handle, it has failed. She keeps hold of the handle and stays still, in profile, looking at the gap. Nobody is outside. Lucy holds her down on the bed across the room and looks toward the door without getting up.
mustBeTrue: a stripe of daylight runs the full height of the doorway and the door leaf stands proud of its frame with its edge and thickness visible, so the door is unmistakably open rather than shut; the gap is only a few inches wide, the handler's hand is still on the handle, and Lucy stays lying on the bed even though the door has opened.
